What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

Two definitions you can use

Learning objective — Explain what software architecture is, using two standard definitions in your own words.

Core principle

Architecture is the structure of a system (its building blocks and the relations between them) together with the decisions and principles behind that structure.

Evidence from the field

Bass, Clements and Kazman (Software Architecture in Practice) define architecture as the set of structures needed to reason about a system: elements, the relations among them, and the properties of both. ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 adds the system's environment and the principles guiding its design and evolution.

Engineering response

When someone asks "what is our architecture?", answer with the main building blocks, how they relate, and the few decisions that explain why.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which part of the two definitions goes beyond "a box-and-line diagram"?

What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

Building blocks and structures

Learning objective — Identify building blocks and relations in a small system.

Core principle

A building block is a part of the system with a clear responsibility, such as a module, a service, a database or a library. Relations say how blocks depend on or talk to each other.

Evidence from the field

Illustrative example. ClinicBook has these blocks: Web App, Booking Service, Calendar Store, Payment Adapter and Reminder Adapter. The Booking Service calls the Calendar Store to hold a slot and the Payment Adapter to take a deposit. Each block can be described without describing the others.

Engineering response

List your system's blocks with one responsibility sentence each. If a block needs two sentences joined by "and also", look closer at it.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Pick one block in a system you know. Can you state its single responsibility in one sentence?

What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

Architecture is decisions

Learning objective — Explain why architecture consists of decisions as well as structure.

Core principle

Structure shows what the system looks like. Decisions explain why it looks that way and what was given up. Without the reasons, the next team cannot tell a deliberate choice from an accident.

Evidence from the field

Nygard's decision records (2011) capture a decision with its context, the choice, and its consequences in a short document. Illustrative example: "We store all appointment times in UTC plus the clinic's time zone name, because clinics sit in several time zones. Consequence: every display needs a conversion."

Engineering response

Record each significant decision in a few lines: context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What would a new colleague lose if only the diagram survived and the reasons were forgotten?

What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

Goals and benefits

Learning objective — Explain the goals and benefits of having a deliberate architecture.

Core principle

The goal of architecture is to meet the requirements, especially quality requirements, and to keep the system understandable and changeable while it grows. The benefit is fewer expensive surprises.

Evidence from the field

Architecture holds the earliest, hardest-to-change decisions (Bass and colleagues). Benefits: shared understanding, early risk detection, a base for planning and estimating.

Engineering response

Justify architecture work by the risks it removes or the changes it makes cheaper, not by the number of diagrams produced.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Name one cost your team paid late because an early structural decision turned out wrong.

What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

Long-term impact

Learning objective — Recognise how early decisions affect a system years later.

Core principle

Structural decisions outlive the people who made them. A choice that is cheap to take in week one can be costly to reverse in year three, because other code and teams come to depend on it.

Evidence from the field

Illustrative example. ClinicBook launches with one clinic in one time zone and stores local times without a zone. When a second clinic opens in another time zone, every stored appointment, report and reminder rule must be revisited. The original choice cost nothing to make and a great deal to undo.

Engineering response

For each major decision ask: how hard would this be to reverse in two years? Take extra care, and extra evidence, with the hard-to-reverse ones.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which decision in your current system would be most expensive to reverse? Why?

What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

What architects do

Learning objective — Describe the main tasks and responsibilities of a software architect.

Core principle

Architects clarify requirements and constraints, design structures, make and record decisions, communicate them, and check that the implementation follows them. They do this with the team, not above it.

Evidence from the field

The tasks are mostly about people and information: asking stakeholders what matters, finding conflicts between goals, explaining trade-offs, reviewing code against decisions, and keeping documentation useful. Drawing is a small share. An architect may or may not hold the title; the tasks must be done by someone.

Engineering response

Treat the architect role as a set of tasks. If nobody owns a task, such as checking decisions against code, the team should assign it explicitly.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which of the tasks above does nobody own in your team today?

What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

Working with other roles

Learning objective — Relate the architect's work to developers, product owners, testers, operations and project managers.

Core principle

Architects depend on others for information and need others to act on decisions. Each role has different concerns, so the same architecture is explained differently to each.

Evidence from the field

Each role needs something different: rules, costly requirements, verifiable targets, failure behaviour, risks. An architect who works alone finds the gaps too late.

Engineering response

Hold short, regular conversations with each role. Ask what they need to know and what would surprise them.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

For one role, say what they need from the architecture and what you need from them.

What Software Architecture Is and What Architects Do

Misconceptions and checklist

Learning objective — Correct four common misconceptions about architecture.

Core principle

Four myths: architecture is just diagrams; the architect decides alone; it is fixed up front and never changes; choosing a framework is the architecture. All four confuse a part of the work with the whole.

Evidence from the field

A framework is one decision, a diagram one way to communicate. Decisions are shared and revised. Checklist: structures named, decisions recorded with reasons, quality goals known, tasks owned.

Engineering response

Run the checklist on your own system and note which line you cannot tick yet.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Which of the four myths have you heard in a real meeting, and how would you now answer it?

quiz.q: Which statement best describes software architecture?
o: The choice of programming language and framework
The job title of the most senior developer
A set of diagrams drawn before coding starts
The structures of a system and the decisions and principles behind them
quiz.why: Definitions by Bass and colleagues and by ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 centre on structures, relations and principles; diagrams only communicate them.

quiz.q: Why record the reasons for an architectural decision?
o: So that the architect cannot be overruled
To reduce the number of building blocks
So that later teams can tell deliberate choices from accidents and judge when to revisit them
Because every standard requires a decision record for each class
quiz.why: Reasons and consequences let future readers judge whether the decision still holds when circumstances change.

quiz.q: Which is a typical architect task?
o: Writing every line of production code
Checking that the implementation follows agreed decisions and discussing deviations
Setting the sprint velocity
Approving each developer's holiday
quiz.why: Checking conformance and discussing deviations belongs to the architect tasks; the others belong to developers or management.

quiz.q: A team picks a web framework and says "the architecture is done". What is wrong with this?
o: A framework is one decision; structure, quality goals and other decisions are still open
Frameworks must be chosen by operations
Nothing, the framework defines all structures
Frameworks are not allowed in architecture
quiz.why: A framework choice is one decision among many and does not replace building blocks or quality goals.

quiz.q: Why do architects talk to testers and operations people?
o: To delegate all design to them
Only to report budget figures
Because they must approve the architect's salary
To learn what must be verifiable and how the system runs and fails, and to share decisions that affect them
quiz.why: Testers and operations have concerns that shape structure, such as verifiable targets and failure handling.

ps: Start with a plain picture. Every system has an architecture, whether anyone designed it or not. The question is whether the structure and the reasons behind it are known and chosen on purpose. A team that can name its building blocks, say why they are cut that way, and say which quality goals drove that cut has an architecture it can talk about. A team that cannot has one by accident.

Architects are not a separate species. The tasks of understanding requirements, designing, deciding, communicating and checking can sit with one person, a small group or the whole team. What matters is that they are done, that the decisions are shared, and that the people building and running the system understand them. Developers with 18 months of team experience already do much of this without the label, for example when they choose a library or split a module.

Watch for the four misconceptions in daily talk. "We have no architecture" usually means no documented one. "The architect decides" usually hides unvoiced concerns of the team. "We designed it up front" ignores that new facts arrive. "We use framework X, so we are done" skips the structure and the quality goals. In each case the answer is the same: name the structures, the decisions and the reasons, and keep them in step with the code.

Illustrative case. ClinicBook starts as one web application with one database, built by four developers for two clinics in the same city. After a year, five clinics in three time zones use it, an external payment provider takes deposits and an external messaging provider sends reminders. Appointments are sometimes double-booked when a receptionist and a patient pick the same slot at the same moment. The team realises that nobody wrote down how slot holds work, why times are stored as they are, or who owns the calendar data. They list their building blocks, write three decision records (time zones, slot holding, payment provider access) and agree that one developer will check pull requests against those records each week. Nothing about this required a new tool or a new title.
Mark your own work against these four criteria. Score each 0, 1 or 2.
head: Criterion
0: Missing
1: Partial
2: Competent
rows: Lists technologies or files instead of blocks
Each block has a single clear responsibility and relations are named
States a choice without reason or alternative
Records context, choice, an alternative and a consequence
Maps every task to an owner and spots unowned tasks
Names a myth without an example
Finds a real example and states the correction
